purpose: Add source-exact public-domain poems, quotations, and an illustration for sermon preparation and presentation slides.

entries.title: Another year with Thee
entries.author: Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.text:
ANOTHER year is dawning !

Dear Master, let it be,
In working or in waiting,

Another year with Thee.
entries.slideText:
ANOTHER year is dawning !

Dear Master, let it be,
In working or in waiting,

Another year with Thee.
entries.sourceTitle: The Poetical Works of Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.rightsBasis: Havergal died in 1879; this circa-1880 edition and its poems are public domain in the United States, and the excerpt was matched against the stored scan OCR.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed opening or closing poem for a new-year message, stewardship review, or call to patient service.
entries.reviewNote: This is devotional poetry, not Scripture; establish doctrine and application from the cited KJV passages.

entries.title: Take my life
entries.author: Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.text:
TAKE my life, and let it be
Consecrated, Lord, to Thee.

Take my moments and my days ;
Let them flow in ceaseless praise.
entries.slideText:
TAKE my life, and let it be
Consecrated, Lord, to Thee.
entries.sourceTitle: The Poetical Works of Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.rightsBasis: Havergal died in 1879; this circa-1880 edition and its poems are public domain in the United States, and the excerpt was matched against the stored scan OCR.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as a concise poetic response to teaching on surrendering one's life, time, and service to God.
entries.reviewNote: This is a hymn stanza. Do not present its wording as Scripture or detach consecration from grace and the governing KJV passage.

entries.title: On the Lord's side
entries.author: Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.text:
WHO is on the Lord's side ?

Who will serve the King ?
Who will be His helpers,

Other lives to bring ?
entries.slideText:
WHO is on the Lord's side ?

Who will serve the King ?
entries.sourceTitle: The Poetical Works of Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.rightsBasis: Havergal died in 1879; this circa-1880 edition and its poems are public domain in the United States, and the excerpt was matched against the stored scan OCR.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed call to loyal service after exposition of the governing passage.
entries.reviewNote: This is devotional poetry. Define Christian service from Scripture rather than from martial imagery alone.

entries.title: True-hearted, whole-hearted
entries.author: Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.text:
TRUE-HEARTED, whole-hearted, faithful and loyal,
King of our lives, by Thy grace we will be

Under Thy standard, exalted and royal,

Strong in Thy strength, we will battle for Thee !
entries.slideText:
TRUE-HEARTED, whole-hearted, faithful and loyal,
King of our lives, by Thy grace we will be
entries.sourceTitle: The Poetical Works of Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.rightsBasis: Havergal died in 1879; this circa-1880 edition and its poems are public domain in the United States, and the excerpt was matched against the stored scan OCR.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed response in messages on steadfastness, faithfulness, or wholehearted service.
entries.reviewNote: This is devotional poetry; use spiritual-warfare language under the KJV text and never to encourage hostility toward people.

entries.title: Like a river glorious
entries.author: Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.text:
LIKE a river glorious

Is God's perfect peace,
Over all victorious

In its bright increase.
Perfect — yet it floweth

Fuller every day ;
Perfect — yet it groweth
Deeper all the way.
entries.slideText:
LIKE a river glorious

Is God's perfect peace,
Over all victorious

In its bright increase.
entries.sourceTitle: The Poetical Works of Frances Ridley Havergal
entries.rightsBasis: Havergal died in 1879; this circa-1880 edition and its poems are public domain in the United States, and the excerpt was matched against the stored scan OCR.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed poetic transition in a message on peace, trust, anxiety, or resting in God.
entries.reviewNote: This is devotional poetry. Explain biblical peace from the cited KJV passages and avoid promising an emotionless Christian life.

entries.title: Illustrations that give no light
entries.author: C. H. Spurgeon
entries.text: Blind windows are fit emblems of illustrations which illustrate nothing, and need themselves to be explained.
entries.slideText: Blind windows are fit emblems of illustrations which illustrate nothing
entries.sourceLocator: Illustrations in Preaching, paragraph beginning 'Illustrations should really cast light'
entries.rightsBasis: Project Gutenberg identifies this edition as public domain in the USA; the excerpt is verified against the stored text.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as a preparation check: if an illustration needs more explanation than the truth it serves, simplify or remove it.
entries.reviewNote: This is homiletic counsel. Scripture, not rhetorical effectiveness, remains the authority and substance of preaching.

entries.title: Jesus must be all in all
entries.author: C. H. Spurgeon
entries.text: Jesus must be all in all: his gospel must be the beginning and end of all our discoursing; parable and poesy must be under his feet, and eloquence must wait upon him as his servant.
entries.slideText: Jesus must be all in all
entries.sourceLocator: Illustrations in Preaching, paragraph beginning 'It may be well to note'
entries.rightsBasis: Project Gutenberg identifies this edition as public domain in the USA; the excerpt is verified against the stored text.
entries.recommendedUse: Use as an attributed reminder that stories, poems, visual art, and rhetoric must serve the message of Christ rather than compete with it.
entries.reviewNote: Use this observation under the cited KJV passages; the quotation is not itself Scripture.

entries.title: The poacher looking for mushrooms
entries.author: C. H. Spurgeon
entries.text: There was an account of a man at Wandsworth, who was discovered, with a gun and a dog, trespassing on some gentleman's preserves, and he said that he was only looking for mushrooms! Can you imagine what the gun and the dog had to do with mushrooms?
entries.slideText: he said that he was only looking for mushrooms!
entries.sourceLocator: Where Can We Find Anecdotes and Illustrations?, current-history example
entries.rightsBasis: Project Gutenberg identifies this edition as public domain in the USA; the excerpt is verified against the stored text.
entries.recommendedUse: Retell briefly to picture the excuses people make when evidence exposes wrongdoing, then move directly to confession and the KJV passage.
entries.reviewNote: Spurgeon adapted a newspaper account as an illustration. Do not use it to shame a particular hearer or as proof of doctrine.
